Experiment 2 (array size 2/10/20): a walkthrough of the results

Regression to the mean in perceptual experience — exploratory, not the main write-up

19 September 2026

About this document

Experiment 2 - array size (2/10/20). Arrays of 2, 10 or 20 coloured squares. Noise was manipulated through the number of squares, each array size using fixed offsets around the mean. Participants reported the colour on a 50-step scale, either the average colour or how red/blue the array felt (experience condition).

This document walks through every result of this experiment: first whether the data and the manipulation are sound, then what they show about regression to the mean (RttM) in perceptual experience. Every number and figure is recomputed from the analysis pipeline when the file is knitted; it is exploratory and not part of the main write-up. True values are the mean of the squares actually shown (EPOC_TRUE_VALUE = "shown").

Two directions of RttM. Forward: given a stimulus, is the report less extreme? (slope of report on true value). Reverse: given a report, was the stimulus less extreme? (the exaggeration claim: extreme experiences overstate the world). Pure noise produces reverse RttM but leaves the forward slope at 1, so a forward slope below 1 needs more than noise.

Bottom line

Array size changes tracking and the forward slope, but through dispersion, not number. Tracking (r .81 / .76 / .77) and the forward slope (.86 / .75 / .81) are lowest at 10 squares, the most dispersed arrays, not at 20 (strict model p < .001, participant level p < .001). About two thirds of the slope change comes from the weaker correlation and one third from narrower reports (ratio p = .046). Extreme reports come from less extreme stimuli at every array size (reverse slope about .67). At the extremes, the comparisons of 2 vs 20 squares go in opposite directions at the two ends (+1.6 units for high reports, −1.5 for low, as given; +1.0 / −1.2 with each participant’s shift removed): for the same report the stimulus was lower at 20 squares at both ends. That is a difference in where reports sit on the scale (possibly linked to the very lopsided 20-square template), not a change in exaggeration. Because 20 squares is not the noisiest level, the level comparisons in this document (first vs last level) are not the noise contrast; 2 vs 10 squares would be.

Key results at a glance (levels in design order; array size is not the order of colour dispersion, see section 2)

Participant flow
Stage Average Experience

  • Trials analysed: average 7,927 (about 92 per participant, mean absolute error 4.93 units); experience 7,107 (about 92 per participant, mean absolute error 4.78 units).
  • Cleaning, identical for all experiments: second sessions dropped; reports of 0 treated as missing (the response scale’s starting value, saved when someone clicks without crossing the scale); RT < 200 ms or > 8 s; ±2.5 SD RT trimming per participant; errors ≥ 30 units; participants keeping < 85% of trials or with Spearman r ≤ .30.

2. Does the manipulation work?

Stimulus checks (true value = mean of the squares shown)
Level Spread within arrays (SD) Spread of true means (SD) Mean true value
2 squares 4.00 6.60 25.16
10 squares 5.95 6.63 25.18
20 squares 5.50 6.63 23.51

The spread of true means across trials is the same at every level, so only the arrays themselves differ between levels. Each level always used the same template of offsets, so the array make-up does not vary within a level and cannot be tested against the report.

Problems found.

  1. Array size does not track colour dispersion. Within-array spreads are about 4.0 / 5.95 / 5.5: the 10-square arrays are the most dispersed, not the 20-square arrays.
  2. Two templates do not average to zero (10 squares +0.2, 20 squares −1.5, and the 20-square template is very lopsided: five squares at −7). This document uses the mean of the squares actually shown as the true value.
  3. 2-square arrays read low (about 3 units below the mean shown), not explained by the colour scale.
  4. Trial order: 2-square trials come slightly earlier in each colour block (task code actually run not checked).
  5. One-step colour offset between stimulus squares and response images (about −1 on all reports; no effect on slopes or comparisons).

Compression shows up as positive values at both ends (reports move toward the middle from both sides); opposite signs at the two ends mean an overall shift of the reports at one level rather than compression.

5. Why the forward slope changes: noise and narrowing

Slope = correlation × (SD of reports / SD of true values); values centred within participant
Level Within-array SD r SD true SD reports SD ratio Slope Calibrated slope (r²) Reverse slope
2 squares 4.00 0.761 6.54 7.38 1.13 0.86 0.58 0.67
10 squares 5.95 0.717 6.61 6.92 1.05 0.75 0.51 0.68
20 squares 5.50 0.726 6.59 7.26 1.10 0.80 0.53 0.66

From 2 squares to 20 squares: log change in slope -0.073, of which 65% from the correlation and 35% from the SD ratio (within participants: correlation p < .001, ratio p = .046). Pure noise would raise the ratio as the correlation falls; a falling ratio is a genuine narrowing of the reports. A calibrated observer’s forward slope would equal r²; slopes above that mean people correct less than their noise warrants, which leaves extreme reports exaggerated (reverse slope = r² / forward slope).

Average true value behind each report value, all levels (reports as given)

Lowest vs highest level, each participant’s constant shift removed

How much more the same extreme report exaggerated its stimulus at 20 squares than at 2 squares (positive = more exaggeration at the higher level)
Extreme reports Participant-level + trial position + position, reweighted
High (≥ 36) as given +1.59, p = .001 +1.55, p = .002 +1.34, p = .006
Low (≤ 14) as given -1.51, p < .001 -1.53, p < .001 -1.17, p < .001

Low (≤ 14) shift removed -1.20, p = .001 -1.17, p = .001 -0.92, p = .011

Only trials with the same report value are compared. “Shift removed” subtracts each participant’s average reporting error at each level first, so a general tendency to answer high or low at one level cannot look like exaggeration at one end; it removes only a constant, not the regression itself. “Reweighted” gives every level the same distribution of true values.

The absolute size of the gap depends on the range of stimuli presented (true values here span about 14–36), so it describes observer and stimulus set together; the differences between levels, which share the same stimulus distribution, carry the claim.
